item.title: Nursery and childcare in the Canton of Vaud: costs and subsidies
item.description: How custody works in the Canton of Vaud: kindergartens, day families, after-school with progressive income rates and available cantonal subsidies.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Childcare in the Canton of Vaud: daycare centers, day families, after-school care with income-based fees - Cantonal subsidies available for low- to middle-income families - Cantonal responsibility: each canton manages pre-school education and extracurricular services - Access procedures to subsidies: income documentation and annual application
## Key facts - **What**: Childcare systems (daycare centers, day families, after-school care) - Where: Canton of Vaud, Switzerland - Who: Cantonal and municipal administrations, public and private providers - Fees: Calculated on a progressive scale based on taxable income - Subsidies: Available at the cantonal level for economic eligibility
In the Canton of Vaud, as in all of Switzerland, childcare and pre-school education are primarily cantonal responsibilities. The Swiss system provides a variety of models: daycare centers (full-time professional facilities), accredited day families (care provided by educators), and after-school care (for school-age children). This variety allows families to choose solutions suited to their context, although the available options and costs vary significantly from canton to canton and between municipalities.
A distinctive feature of Switzerland is the progressive approach to childcare fees: most cantons, including Vaud, apply pricing scales calculated on the family's income. This means that a family with a higher taxable income pays a higher fee compared to a family with a lower income, following principles of economic progressivity. In addition to fees, cantons offer public subsidies to reduce the financial burden on low- to middle-income families. These subsidies are important socio-economic policy tools: they facilitate access to education, support work-family balance, and promote equity in the quality of care.
To understand the situation in the Canton of Vaud, it is essential to distinguish between levels of governance. The cantonal administration sets the general guidelines (curricula, hygiene and health standards, educator credentials), while municipalities manage local planning and co-finance services through detailed links on childcare. The consequence is that even within Vaud, fees and the availability of subsidies differ between municipalities. An urban municipality like Lausanne may offer a greater variety of public services compared to a rural municipality, with direct impacts on the availability of places and fees applied. ### How do progressive fee scales work?
In the Swiss childcare system, progressive fees do not follow a single national model: each canton, and sometimes each municipality, applies its own criteria. The underlying principle remains constant: the family contributes according to its economic capacity. A higher taxable income results in a higher monthly cost; a lower income results in a reduced fee or sometimes a symbolic minimum rate.
Factors influencing the cost of childcare include the number of children in care (often the fee for the second child is reduced), the hours of use (full-time, part-time, specific days), the age of the child (the ranges 0-2 years and 2-4 years often have different fees), and the type of facility (public vs. private daycare, accredited family daycare, after-school care). In the canton of Vaud, as in other progressive cantons, municipal administrations have calculation tools—sometimes digital—that allow families to simulate the monthly fee once income, number of children, and details of the desired care are entered. This transparency is useful for family economic planning.
### Variability between facilities and municipalities
Not all families have access to the same services. In urban municipalities of Vaud, the availability of places in public daycare centers is often higher than in rural municipalities. Municipal public facilities tend to apply lower fees compared to private services, thanks to public co-financing. A family that does not find a place in a public daycare center may have to resort to a private facility, with significantly higher costs.
Accredited family daycare (certified home-based care) also has variable fees. Generally, the hourly cost of family daycare is lower than a daycare center, but the hourly flexibility is different and not all municipalities offer the same level of quality control or subsidies for this service. After-school care, a less costly service because it is generally less specialized, remains a significant expense for families with school-age children. Here too, progressive fees based on income are the norm in the canton of Vaud.
### Economic impact: hypothetical scenario
A hypothetical scenario illustrates the economic importance. A single-parent family working full-time with a moderate taxable income needs full-time care for an 18-month-old child. In a similar scenario, the monthly fee could represent a significant percentage of the family income—up to 15-20% or more—without subsidies. With cantonal subsidies, this percentage would be considerably reduced, transforming the economic accessibility of childcare. The difference between access to subsidies and lack of subsidies is therefore decisive for the family budget and for the ability to maintain employment. For this reason, understanding the methods of accessing subsidies is essential for economic planning.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ## How to access childcare subsidies
In the Canton of Vaud, as in many other Swiss cantons, access to childcare subsidies is subject to clear eligibility criteria, although specific to each municipality. Subsidies are generally reserved for low- to middle-income families (defined by taxable income thresholds per household), working or studying parents (to encourage participation in the labor market), and stable residents of the canton (Swiss citizens, holders of a residence permit, or equivalent situations). Some cantons extend subsidies to parents engaged in job search or training activities, recognizing that childcare is a prerequisite for economic participation.
### Access Procedure: Main Steps
The access path to subsidies generally follows these steps: **first**, contact the municipality of residence — the social affairs or education office provides information on available subsidies, income thresholds, and required documents. Second, gather documentation, which generally includes income tax returns (copy of federal or cantonal declaration), employment documentation (employer certificate, employment contract), household composition (cohabitation certificate), and proof of childcare (contract with daycare, family daycare, after-school care).
Third, submit the application within the deadlines specified by the municipality — often annual — by submitting the complete file. Fourth, the municipal administration verifies eligibility and calculates the subsidy amount based on income and agreed rates. Fifth, if approved, the subsidy is paid monthly or at a defined frequency (monthly, quarterly, annually).
### Specific Information and Deadlines
Each municipality in Vaud has a dedicated administrative structure for family support. It is advisable to contact the local municipal administration (social assistance office or education), a one-stop shop for families if available, or consult cantonal websites that often provide detailed guides, forms, and cost simulators. Subsidies are not automatic nor permanent: most cantons require annual renewal of the application, with updating of income documentation. It is important to respect deadlines to avoid losing acquired rights. Delays in submitting the application may result in the loss of retroactive subsidy payments, with non-recoverable costs.
### Practical Implications and Action
Access to subsidies significantly transforms the economic accessibility of childcare. A family benefiting from a subsidy sees the monthly fee reduced from a significant percentage of income to a more manageable one. For many families, the subsidy is the difference between being able to work and having to stay at home, with direct implications on income, career, and economic independence. Discover how to use the tools to simulate childcare costs through the available calculator, or delve into [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living) solutions for an integrated view of the family budget. For concrete actions: contact your municipality within the first quarter of the fiscal year to receive information on the next cycle's subsidies; gather income and employment documents promptly; calculate the estimated amount through municipal simulators; submit the application respecting official deadlines; keep track of administrative communication for any follow-ups.

item.title: Scholarships canton Vaud: requirements and amounts
item.description: How to access scholarships and loans for study in the canton of Vaud: economic requirements, academic merit, maximum amounts and application procedure.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Scholarships in the canton of Vaud are awarded based on merit and economic situation - The canton of Vaud offers both grants and subsidized study loans - The application must be submitted to the dedicated cantonal office - Requirements and maximum amounts depend on the economic situation and type of training
## Key facts - **What**: Scholarships and study loans in the canton of Vaud - Where: Canton of Vaud, French-speaking Switzerland - Who: Cantonal administration of Vaud (responsible for education) - Requirements: Economic situation, academic merit, residence in the canton - Amounts: Variable according to the level of study and economic situation (details at the cantonal office)
### The study support system in the canton of Vaud
The canton of Vaud offers a comprehensive system of scholarships and study loans to support access to higher education and continuing education. These support measures fall under the competence of the Swiss cantonal administrations, in line with the principle of subsidiarity that characterizes the Swiss system: education is a matter managed by the individual cantons, each with its own laws and ordinances.
As in all Swiss cantonal scholarship systems, the measures are granted taking into account the economic situation of the family and the academic merit of the applicant. In the canton of Vaud, the granting of a scholarship is subject to a combined evaluation of economic and academic factors, allowing the identification of those with the greatest financial need and academic potential.
### Types of available aid
The canton of Vaud provides two main types of aid: - Grants: aid that does not require repayment and is awarded based on the overall assessment of the applicant - Subsidized loans: amounts lent at interest rates lower than the commercial market, intended to be repaid after completing the training
Many beneficiaries receive a combination of the two: a partial grant and a subsidized loan to cover the remaining financial need. This flexibility allows applicants to adapt the financial support to their personal situation and future income prospects.
### Who can apply
The criteria for accessing Vaud scholarships generally include residence in the canton, Swiss or European citizenship (with possible variations for valid residence permits), enrollment in a recognized training program (high school, apprenticeship, university, specialized school), and passing an academic merit test. The economic situation of the family is a determining factor: scholarships are awarded primarily to those with the least ability to self-finance their studies. ### Analysis: How the System Works and Practical Implications
### Economic and Academic Requirements
In the canton of Vaud, as in other Swiss cantons, the allocation of scholarships follows a dual evaluation model: the family must demonstrate an economic situation that justifies support, but the applicant must also present a sufficient academic profile. This dual evaluation reflects the objective of the Swiss system: to support those with academic potential but limited economic resources.
Family income is calculated according to standardized methodologies, which consider: - Gross and net family income (from the previous 2 years) - Assets (savings, real estate, bank accounts) - Number of dependents - Recognized ordinary expenses (housing, LAMal health insurance premiums, transportation, living expenses)
Each canton sets its own income thresholds, above which the granting of scholarships becomes less likely or is refused. These thresholds vary significantly between cantons, reflecting the different fiscal capacities of the individual Swiss cantons.
### Maximum Amounts and Calculation Methods
In the Swiss context, the amounts of cantonal scholarships generally cover part of the study costs (tuition fees, books, equipment) and, in some cases, part of the food and accommodation costs. The annual maximum amounts vary significantly between cantons: some cantons with greater fiscal resources (Zurich, Geneva, Basel) tend to offer higher scholarship amounts compared to cantons with fewer resources.
The canton of Vaud, as a canton of French-speaking Switzerland, has its own fiscal and financial capacity. The maximum amounts and calculation methods of the scholarship are set by cantonal ordinances and are available at the competent office. It is important to emphasize that the amounts are not fixed but calculated individually based on financial need: two students with similar academic merit may receive different scholarship amounts if their family economic situation is different.
### Implications for Educational Mobility
Access to scholarships directly affects a family's ability to invest in their children's education. In a context where university tuition fees in Switzerland are moderate compared to other Western countries but still significant, cantonal scholarships remain an essential tool for social inclusion.
Particularly relevant is the support for young people who choose vocational training paths (apprenticeships): in Switzerland, this path is prestigious and widely spread, but some require economic resources for accommodation, materials, and transportation. The scholarships of the canton of Vaud also cover these alternative paths to university, allowing young people to access excellent training regardless of immediate family resources.
### Deadlines and Timing in the Academic Calendar
Scholarship applications must be submitted by specific deadlines set by the canton. Generally, the submission window coincides with course enrollment (June-August), but this information must be verified with the official office, as deadlines vary from year to year. Delays in submitting the application usually result in the evaluation being postponed to the following academic year, forcing the student to self-finance for the first year.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### Action: How to apply step by step
### Phase 1: Inform and verify eligibility
The first step is to verify if you meet the basic eligibility criteria at the dedicated cantonal office. Most cantons (including Vaud) provide an online preliminary questionnaire or self-assessment guide to understand the level of admissibility.
Essential elements to verify: - Residence in the canton of Vaud (generally required for at least 2 years, but this rule varies according to the cantonal ordinance) - Swiss, European citizenship, or valid residence permit - Confirmed enrollment in a recognized school/university/apprenticeship center - Family economic situation below cantonal thresholds
### Phase 2: Gather the required documentation
Once eligibility is confirmed, you need to prepare the required documentation. Typically, this includes: - Family income statements (last 2 tax years) — this is the fundamental document for calculating the need - Certificate of residence in the canton of Vaud - School certificates and academic merit certificates - Letter of enrollment in a training institution (university, high school, apprenticeship center) - Eventually, documentation related to real estate, bank accounts, or other assets
This information is used to calculate the amount of the scholarship and to evaluate whether the applicant falls within the financial need defined by the canton. It is crucial to present accurate and up-to-date documents: errors or omissions can significantly delay the evaluation.
### Phase 3: Fill out the application form
The application form must be filled out at the cantonal office or downloaded from the official website. The form asks for: - Biographical data of the applicant and family - Precise details on the economic situation (gross income, net income, assets, number of dependents) - Information on the type and level of study (high school, university, apprenticeship, specialized school) - Choice between a grant and/or subsidized loan (or combination) - IBAN bank details for the disbursement of the scholarship - Motivation and professional prospects (some cantons require a brief training project)
The form must be filled out carefully, as incomplete or contradictory information can result in the rejection of the application.
### Phase 4: Submit by the official deadline
The submission must be made by the official deadline, which generally falls between June and August. It is advisable to submit at least 2-3 weeks before the deadline to avoid technical surprises (server congestion, transmission errors, reception problems).
### Phase 5: Receive the decision and disbursement of the scholarship
The cantonal office examines the application and communicates the decision (approval, partial approval, rejection) within the established deadlines, generally 6-8 weeks. If approved, the scholarship is disbursed according to the agreed modalities: semi-annual or annual bank transfer, typically in November and May.
### Contacts and next steps
For specific information on maximum amounts, exact deadlines, and details on the requirements of the canton of Vaud, it is necessary to contact the dedicated cantonal administration directly. The official websites of the cantons provide contacts, complete forms, and operational guides.
An essential resource for planning the financing of studies is the [financial support calculator](nav:calculator), which allows you to estimate the total financial need and plan the study path based on the actual family budget.

item.title: At school only 4 days, the experiment (for now) convinces
item.description: For three weeks, in Belp, in the Canton of Bern, a new pilot project has been underway with 4 days of school and 6 weeks of vacation.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - School experiment in Belp, Canton Bern - 4 days of school, 6 weeks of vacation - Parents and children enthusiastic
## Key facts - **What**: School experiment in Belp - When: For three weeks - Where: Belp, Canton Bern - Who: 21 children and their families - Amount: Not specified
A new pilot project has been underway for three weeks in Belp, Canton Bern. Less holiday-related stress, less attendance issues during after-school hours, and fewer trips between school, lunch, and home. For the 21 children of the Bernese school, the traditional lessons leave room for continuous supervision, even during the lunch break. Children attend school four days a week, from Monday to Thursday, instead of five but, in return, have only six weeks of vacation per year instead of thirteen.
The testimony of two mothers
"It was a good start, my daughter likes to go there," says Lisa, mother of one of the 21 children. Almost every day his daughter comes home with "a lot of experiences". And there's room for kids' ideas, too.
"She can't wait to attend the cooking class." For her daughter, in fact, one of the most pleasant moments is cooking together with the others. Since the children stay at school during the lunch break, they also help prepare the food: "She is always happy when she is assigned to the cooking group".
Longer days, but more energy.
Manuela, whose six-year-old daughter also participates ## Practical Implications
The school experiment at Belp could have significant implications for the Swiss education system. Reducing school days to four days could lead to better time management for families, reducing stress related to after-school hours and holidays. However, it is important to monitor the impact of longer days on children, especially younger ones, to ensure they do not become overly fatigued.
## Comparison with the traditional model
The traditional model includes five days of school and thirteen weeks of vacation. The new experiment, on the other hand, offers four days of school and only six weeks of vacation. This change could affect the daily routine of families, allowing them to have one day off per week for activities and relaxation. However, it is necessary to assess whether the shorter holidays will be sufficient for rest and unstructured family time.
## Possible scenarios
If the experiment proves positive, it could be adopted by other schools in Switzerland. This could lead to a reform of the education system, with a greater focus on the quality of daily life of children and their families. However, it is important to conduct further studies to better understand the long-term effects of this new model.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ## Concrete actions
If you are interested in learning more about this school experiment, you can visit the Belp school's official website for more information. In addition, you can participate in online discussions and educational forums to share your opinions and experiences with other parents and educators.
## Useful tools
To deepen your understanding of the Swiss education system and its implications, you can use the [calcolatore stipendio](nav:calculator) to assess how new education policies might affect your family budget. In addition, you can consult the educational guides for useful tips and resources for managing time and extracurricular activities.
## Conclusion
The school experiment in Belp represents an innovative step towards a more balanced management of school time and holidays. Although it is still too early to draw definitive conclusions, the first testimonies of parents and children are promising. We will continue to monitor the development of this project and provide updates on any changes in the Swiss education system.

item.title: Residence permit B Canton Zug: requirements and renewal
item.description: Guide to residence permit B in Zug: how the renewable permit works, what federal and cantonal requirements to follow, documents and renewal procedure.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Renewable permit B for residence in Switzerland - Federal (SEM) and cantonal management of the renewal - Federal and cantonal requirements for resident aliens
## Key facts - **What**: Residence permit for long-term residence in Switzerland - Type: Category B renewable without maximum limit of years - Where: Canton of Zug (like all Swiss cantons) - Who manages: Federal State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) and cantonal administration - Validity: Renewable on request at the scheduled deadlines - Requirements: Check at the cantonal migration office of Zug
Residence permit B is a federal category that allows permanent residence in Switzerland and is renewable according to the procedures of the canton of competence. In the Canton of Zug, as in all Swiss cantons, management follows both federal and cantonal regulations. The State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) sets the national criteria, while the cantonal administration applies them locally. Those who hold a B permit enjoy long-term residence and work rights, unlike the L permit which allows short stays of up to 1 year.
### Residence permit B in Switzerland The B permit is a national category that allows long-term residence. It differs from the L permit (short duration, maximum 1 year) and the C permit (domicile, usually granted after 10 years of continuous residence for non-European citizens, 5 for EU/EFTA citizens). ### Social and tax implications of the B permit The B residence permit entails specific rights and obligations at the Swiss level. Those residing with a B permit must ensure mandatory health insurance coverage (LAMal) within 3 months of arrival in Switzerland; premiums vary according to the canton of residence, age, and chosen deductible. In the Canton of Zug, LAMal premiums are calculated in canton brackets, with the possibility of reduction through cantonal subsidies intended for low-income families. Additionally, the B permit requires the payment of social contributions: AVS/AI (Old-Age and Survivors' Insurance / Disability Insurance) for mandatory pension insurance, at a rate of 5.3% borne by the employee (to which is added the 5.3% of the employer, for a total of 10.6%). Those classified as stable employees also contribute to an LPP (Professional Pension) plan, according to progressive contribution tables: 7% for employees aged 25-34, 10% for 35-44, 15% for 45-54, 18% for 55+ until the reference age. It is not necessary to contribute on the entire salary: there is a coordination deduction that excludes an initial portion of the salary from LPP.
### Differences between B, C, and L permits Those holding a C permit (domicile) enjoy similar rights to the B permit but with greater legal stability. Domicile is generally renewable without a defined expiration date (after 10 years of continuous residence for foreigners, 5 for EU/EFTA citizens), while the B permit has periodic expirations and renewal upon application. In some cantons, the renewal of B occurs every 5 years, in others every 2 years; the Canton of Zug follows specific cantonal regulations (details at the competent migration office). The L permit, intended for short stays up to 1 year, is not renewable: it is aimed at temporary professionals, researchers, trainees, and other temporary cases. Those working as employees with a B permit pay AVS/AI contributions and, if classified, LPP. Furthermore, the B permit entails the obligation to submit an annual income tax return (federal direct tax, IFD) and to pay cantonal and communal taxes according to the rates of the canton of residence: Zug has its own tax rate, with municipalities applying different multipliers on the cantonal tax base.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to renew the B permit in Zug: practical procedure To renew the B residence permit in the Canton of Zug, the first step is to check the expiry date on the document itself. It is recommended to contact the competent migration office at least 2-3 months before the expiry date, to allow time to gather the required documentation. The cantonal office will communicate the exact list of documents during the preliminary consultation; generally, it includes documentation related to the employment situation (employment contract or letter from the employer), housing (lease agreement, rent payments), income tax return for the previous year, and certificates of good conduct. It is necessary to submit a renewal application filled out according to the form provided by the cantonal administration, together with the above-mentioned documentation. The migration office of the Canton of Zug will evaluate the application and generally communicate the outcome within a few weeks of receiving the complete application. During the waiting period, the current permit remains valid if submitted within the prescribed deadlines; some cantons issue a provisional certificate to ensure continuity of rights during the evaluation procedure.
### Useful information and resources For official information on renewing the B residence permit in the Canton of Zug, the main reference is the migration office (Migrationsamt) of the Canton of Zug, which provides forms, updated lists of documents, and opening hours. At the federal level, the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) publishes general guidelines and national criteria on the website www.sem.admin.ch. If you reside in Zug and have doubts about your tax situation related to the residence permit, the [tax return](nav:tax-return) is a mandatory step every year; if you want a preliminary estimate of your federal direct tax obligations, use our [tax calculator](nav:calculator). Additionally, to deepen the pension situation (AVS, LPP, third pillar), consult our [pension tool](nav:pension). For information on the [health insurance (LAMal)](nav:health) mandatory in the Canton of Zug, contact the insurance institutions to compare the available options.

item.title: Inheritance and donation tax of the canton of Glarus: the rates
item.description: In the Canton of Glarus, inheritance and gift tax follows an autonomous cantonal regime with rates that vary by degree of kinship and exemptions for spouse and descendants. Practical guide and declaration procedure.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - In the Canton of Glarus, inheritance tax is regulated exclusively by its own cantonal laws - Rates and exemptions vary depending on the degree of kinship between the heir and the deceased - Declaration within the deadlines set by the canton, to the competent administration
## Key facts - **What**: Cantonal inheritance and gift tax - Where: Canton of Glarus, Switzerland - Who: Cantonal administration (tax office) - When: Within the deadlines set by the cantonal ordinance - Scope: Varies by degree of kinship (spouse, descendants, collaterals, strangers)
In Switzerland, there is no federal inheritance tax: the competence is entirely decentralized to the cantons. The Canton of Glarus, like the other cantons, has legislated autonomously on the taxation of inheritances and gifts. The result is a mosaic of different regimes: those who inherit in the Canton of Glarus pay rates determined by Glarus law, different from those of Zurich, Geneva, Ticino or other cantons. Unlike income and wealth taxation — where there is a federal direct tax that adds to cantonal and municipal taxes — for inheritance the regime remains purely cantonal. No revenue goes to Bern: everything remains within the administrative competence of the canton.
In the Canton of Glarus, inheritance and gift tax follows a central principle: rates and exemptions depend on the degree of kinship between the deceased (or donor) and the heir. As throughout Switzerland, the law provides exemptions for the surviving spouse and descendants (children, grandchildren). This reflects the principle that the transfer of assets within the immediate family should receive more favorable tax treatment than inheritances from collaterals or strangers.
### Structure of the Glarus regime
Anyone facing an inheritance in the Canton of Glarus must submit a declaration of the inherited assets to the cantonal administration within the deadlines set by the local ordinance. These deadlines, the methods of calculating the tax, the exemption thresholds and the possibilities of contestation are matters of exclusively cantonal competence. For this reason, anyone who inherits or receives a gift in Glarus must contact the cantonal tax office directly to learn the specific details of their tax position and the rates applied to their case. ### How the tax calculation works in the Canton of Glarus
The inheritance tax in the Canton of Glarus follows a logical and progressive procedure. First, the total value of inherited assets is established: real estate, bank accounts, securities, life insurance, companies, vehicles. This gross value constitutes the tax base. Subsequently, the exemption and deduction rules provided for by cantonal law are applied. This is where the degree of kinship comes into play.
The surviving spouse, in most Swiss cantons, enjoys a total or very significant exemption — often 100%. Direct descendants (children) are entitled to important deductions, frequently scalar based on the number of heirs. Second-degree descendants (grandchildren) have reduced rights compared to children. Collaterals (brothers, sisters, cousins) have minor exemptions. Outsiders (unrelated people) pay full rates with almost no deduction. In the Glarus Canton this general principle applies, but the specific numerical values are fixed by the Glarus cantonal law.
### Donations: the complement of succession
Alongside inheritance tax (which applies to death), the Canton of Glarus also taxes living donations. Again, rates and exemptions depend on the degree of kinship between donor and beneficiary. A donation from a parent to a child is generally less taxed than a donation to a third party.
## Useful tools for your case To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). ### Practical procedure: what to do in the Canton of Glarus
When a death occurs involving assets in the Canton of Glarus, or when a significant donation is made, the heir or beneficiary has a legal obligation to submit a declaration to the cantonal tax office within the deadlines set by local regulations.
**First step: gather documentation**. You will need the death certificate (issued by the commune of the place of death), a complete and detailed inventory of the inherited assets, property appraisals, the latest bank statements, a certified copy of the will (if any), and any registered donation deeds. This collection can take weeks and sometimes months, especially if the assets are spread across multiple locations.
Second step: contact the cantonal tax office. It is essential to ask which forms to use, which deadlines to respect precisely, whether specialized consultations (notary, accountant) are required, and what the specific rates are based on the heir's degree of kinship. The administration can provide details on tax matters and the correct procedure.
Third step: submit the declaration according to the cantonal deadlines. Generally, the deadline is a few months from the date of death. Failure to comply results in penalties and late interest. The declaration must indicate the total value of the assets, the degree of kinship of each heir, the deductions and exemptions applicable, and the calculation of the tax due based on the cantonal rates.
### When to consult a professional
Although anyone can submit a succession declaration independently, complex situations require specialized advice. If the succession includes businesses, properties in multiple cantons, significant insurance benefits, or if the heirs are numerous and disagree on the division of assets, it is advisable to consult a notary or an accountant authorized to practice in the Canton of Glarus. The costs of a consultation are often lower than the tax savings that an expert can achieve through succession planning and correct interpretation of cantonal law.
Additionally, a professional ensures that all deadlines are met and that the declaration is completed correctly, avoiding disputes and subsequent checks by the tax administration. To plan your situation and better understand the tax aspects of succession, access our [tax calculator](nav:calculator).

item.title: Canton Glarus Driving License: Conversion and Exams
item.description: How to convert your foreign driver's license in the canton of Glarus: complete procedure, theoretical-practical exams and mandatory courses for those who move to Switzerland.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Foreign driving license convertible in the canton of Glarus through administrative procedure - Theoretical and practical exams required according to the applicant's nationality - Mandatory courses integrate the conversion process - Contact the competent traffic office for specific details
- **What**: Conversion of foreign driving license to Switzerland - Where: Traffic office of the canton of Glarus - For whom: Residents with a valid foreign driving license - Procedures: Theory, practice, courses according to nationality - Requirements: Original driving license, identity document, cantonal residence
Anyone arriving in the canton of Glarus with a foreign driving license must undergo an administrative conversion procedure. Although Switzerland widely recognizes foreign driving licenses, the canton requires the completion of specific steps, which may include theoretical exams, practical exams, and mandatory safe driving courses according to Swiss standards.
The procedure is not identical for all new residents. The process mainly varies based on the nationality and the country of origin of the driving license. Some citizens from certain countries obtain direct conversion without additional exams, while others must undergo theoretical-practical tests and follow mandatory training courses designated by the canton.
In the canton of Glarus, the procedure is managed by the cantonal traffic office (Verkehrsamt). This office is the official reference for anyone wishing to convert their foreign driving license into a valid Swiss driving license within the cantonal territory. Moving to the canton implies understanding not only the administrative procedures but also the [cost of living and local opportunities](nav:cost-of-living) that characterize the region.
The timing depends on multiple factors: completeness of documentation, need for exams, attendance of mandatory courses, and scheduling of appointments at the office. Therefore, it is advisable to start the procedure immediately after arrival, respecting the deadlines set by the cantonal legislation.
### Swiss recognition of foreign driving licenses
Switzerland, through the individual cantons, has entered into reciprocal agreements with various countries for the direct recognition of driving licenses. These agreements simplify the procedure for citizens from specific nations, allowing conversion without additional exams. However, for citizens from countries not included in the agreements, the path is more restricted and requires the completion of all tests prescribed by the cantonal legislation of Glarus. ### Theoretical exam in the conversion of the driving license
When requested, the theoretical exam verifies knowledge of Swiss traffic regulations, including the specificities of the canton of Glarus. It is not just abstract knowledge, but concrete familiarity with road signs, speed limits, right of way, and behaviors specifically provided by Swiss law. The exam takes place at the competent traffic office and covers Swiss federal regulations and cantonal particularities.
The theoretical exam should not be underestimated: it requires serious preparation and a deep understanding of traffic rules. Many candidates follow preparatory courses or use study materials provided by accredited entities to familiarize themselves with the exam format and required contents. The test includes multiple-choice questions and may include sections on emergency behavior, special vehicles, and complex traffic situations.
### Practical exam and road checks
The practical exam, where required, takes place behind the wheel of an official vehicle under the supervision of an authorized examiner. The examiner verifies the candidate's ability to operate safely in the Swiss road context, including the specific topography and traffic of the canton. The practical exam includes maneuvers in the city, on extra-urban roads, and may include highway routes depending on the license category requested.
During the exam, the examiner evaluates not only the technical driving skills but also the respect for regulations, awareness of risks, and adaptation to [Swiss transport and mobility systems](nav:transport). Those who do not pass the exam on the first attempt have the right to retake it on subsequent dates, coordinated by the traffic office. The examiner provides feedback on the aspects not passed to allow for targeted preparation.
### Mandatory courses and safety training
Mandatory courses represent an essential component of the conversion of foreign licenses in Switzerland. They are not just theoretical lessons but road safety training programs according to Swiss standards. Typical contents include eco-driving, accident prevention, emergency behavior, fatigue management while driving, and adaptation to Swiss transport systems.
Attendance at the courses is a prerequisite for completing the procedure. In the canton of Glarus, courses are offered by accredited providers according to a predetermined schedule. The traffic office coordinates with the candidate the available dates, ensuring that the courses take place before the completion of the conversion procedure. The duration and structure of the courses vary according to the license category and the nationality of the applicant.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Step-by-step procedure in the canton of Glarus
**Step 1: Gather documentation** — Prepare the original foreign driver's license, valid ID (passport or ID card), proof of residence in the canton of Glarus (civil registry extract or lease agreement), and medical certificate if required by your individual situation or age. Check with the office if other documents are necessary.
Step 2: Contact the traffic office — The competent cantonal office (Verkehrsamt of the canton of Glarus) is the reference point. It provides official forms, clarifies which exams and courses are required for your specific situation based on nationality and license category, and assigns available exam dates.
Step 3: Attend mandatory courses (if applicable) — Some cases require training courses before the practical exam. Coordinate with the office to attend courses at accredited providers in the canton and respect the deadlines for attendance.
Step 4: Take exams (theoretical and practical, if necessary) — The theoretical exam takes place at the traffic office on set dates. The practical exam is conducted on the road with an official vehicle and a certified examiner, usually on weekdays at predetermined times.
Step 5: Receive the Swiss driver's license — Once all requirements are met, the office issues the Swiss driver's license valid in the canton and recognized throughout the Confederation. The Swiss license allows free circulation throughout the national territory.
### Important deadlines and timelines
The entire process can take from a few weeks to several months, depending on the office's workload, the assignment of available exam dates, and the mandatory attendance of courses. Some cantons set deadlines within which the foreign license must be converted or declared invalid for driving in Swiss territory.
It is advisable to start the procedure immediately after arriving in the canton of Glarus. Waiting too long could complicate the legal situation of driving in the canton and create administrative inconveniences. If you drive without having started the conversion after the allowed times, you risk fines and insurance invalidity.
### Contacts and resources
For precise details on deadlines, costs, exam calendar, and specific requirements for your nationality, contact the traffic office of the canton of Glarus directly. The information varies based on your individual profile and the origin of the license.
If you are considering moving to the canton of Glarus, also evaluate [local livability and quality of life](nav:livability): factors such as housing costs, accessibility to services, and job opportunities significantly influence the decision to move and integration into the new territory.

item.title: Apprenticeship and training in the Canton of Vaud: a practical guide
item.description: How to find an internship in the Canton of Vaud, salary, apprenticeship contract and professional maturity according to Swiss federal law.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Apprenticeship lasts 3-4 years depending on the chosen trade - Combines practical training in the company and theoretical teaching at school - Salary established by the apprenticeship contract, not national - Professional maturity allows continuation of studies after apprenticeship
## Key facts - **What**: Theoretical-practical training program in recognized trades - When: Three or four years according to the chosen professional profile - Where: Training company plus cantonal vocational school - Who: Apprentice, employer, cantonal educational system - Amount: Salary agreed in the apprenticeship contract
### The structure of apprenticeship in Switzerland
In Switzerland, apprenticeship is one of the pillars of the educational system. In the Canton of Vaud, as in the rest of the country, vocational training combines theoretical teaching in vocational school and practical training on the field in a training company. This dual model allows apprentices to acquire concrete skills while continuing their general education.
The duration of the apprenticeship varies according to the chosen trade, typically between three and four years. During this period, the apprentice is subject to federal labor regulations, which include hourly limits and fundamental rights. According to the Swiss regulatory framework, young people under 20 are entitled to a minimum of five weeks of annual leave, while those over 20 benefit from a minimum of four weeks.
The Canton of Vaud, like other Swiss cantons, manages the offer of vocational schools and coordinates with training companies to ensure apprenticeship opportunities in various economic sectors. The responsibility for training is shared between the federal state, which sets professional standards, and the cantons, which organize the administration of school training.
### Salary and apprenticeship contract
The apprentice's salary is not set at the federal level but is agreed upon in the apprenticeship contract between the young person and the employer. In the Canton of Vaud, as in the rest of Switzerland, the apprenticeship contract is the legal document that regulates the rights and duties of both parties.
The contract specifies the duration of the apprenticeship, the monthly or hourly salary, working hours, the apprentice's responsibilities, and the modalities of attendance of theoretical training. Make sure the contract contains all these elements before signing, as it represents the legal basis of the apprenticeship relationship. For more information on salary scenarios and tax deductions, consult the [salary calculator](nav:calculator). ### Research and Application Channels in the Canton of Vaud
Finding an apprenticeship position in the Canton of Vaud can be done through various channels. Many companies that train apprentices advertise their opportunities directly on national job portals or through industry federations. The Canton of Vaud, through its professional guidance offices and secondary schools, provides resources and advice to guide young people in their search.
The cantonal chambers of commerce and industry, as well as the Swiss professional associations in various sectors, maintain databases of training companies willing to accept apprentices. It is advisable to start the search at least 12-18 months before the desired start date, as many companies select apprentices in advance. This period allows for evaluating more opportunities and making an informed choice.
### Content of the Apprenticeship Contract
Once a company willing to train has been identified, the apprenticeship contract is signed. This document must contain essential elements: the name of the apprentice and the employer, the trade for which training is provided, the total duration of the apprenticeship (usually 3-4 years), the start date, the remuneration for each year of apprenticeship, weekly working hours, and days off.
The probationary period, typically the first 1-3 months, allows both the apprentice and the employer to assess compatibility. During the probationary period, both parties can terminate the contract with reduced notice periods, often without notice or with a few days' notice. After the probationary period, the termination conditions follow the Swiss federal labor regulations: in the first year, termination is possible with one or two months' notice, from the second to the ninth year with two months, and from the tenth year with three months.
### Organization of School Training
The school component of the apprenticeship takes place at the cantonal vocational school. In the Canton of Vaud, as in other cantons, vocational schools offer theoretical teaching, common subjects (language and mathematics), and specialized disciplines related to the trade. Generally, apprentices attend vocational school one or two days a week, while the remaining days are spent working at the training company.
This dual system allows for continuous learning and progressive acquisition of both theoretical and practical skills. Attendance at the vocational school is mandatory and is part of the apprentice's rights and duties. The costs of attendance are covered by the cantonal public system.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Professional Maturity and Continuing Education
Upon completing the apprenticeship, the apprentice obtains the Federal Vocational Education and Training Certificate (EFZ) in the chosen trade. A significant advantage of the Swiss system is the possibility of obtaining professional maturity during or after the apprenticeship, which opens access to higher education courses at Universities of Applied Sciences (UAS).
Professional maturity includes general subjects (languages, mathematics, sciences) alongside specialized disciplines and requires additional work compared to the standard apprenticeship path. In the Canton of Vaud, as in other Swiss cantons, attendance at professional maturity is funded by the public sector, although the responsibility for organization falls to the cantonal system. Admission requirements and schedules vary slightly between cantons.
### Apprentice Rights According to Federal Law
Apprentices, like all workers in Switzerland, enjoy federal legal protection. Maximum working hours are set at 45 hours per week for sectors such as industry, offices, and retail, while other sectors can reach 50 hours per week. Breaks and rest periods are regulated to protect young workers from the risks of fatigue and dangerous working conditions.
Health insurance (LAMal/KVG) is mandatory for all residents in Switzerland, including apprentices, and must be taken out within three months of starting work. Contributions for federal social insurance (AVS/AHV and AI) begin on the first day of work: the employer pays the social contributions, while the apprentice contributes a share of the wages. These elements are an integral part of the Swiss social protection package.
### Practical Procedure: Checklist to Start an Apprenticeship
Summarizing the concrete steps for those wishing to start an apprenticeship in the Canton of Vaud:
1. Identify trades of interest and consult regional or national databases of training companies. 2. Prepare a complete application with CV, cover letter, and, if possible, school references. 3. Contact training companies directly or respond to apprenticeship offers published online. 4. Once a company is identified, carefully check the apprenticeship contract before signing, ensuring it clearly specifies remuneration, hours, duration, and responsibilities. 5. Register with the cantonal vocational school (the employer will support this step). 6. Take out mandatory health insurance within three months of starting the apprenticeship. 7. Inquire at the Canton of Vaud's career guidance office regarding opportunities for professional maturity if you wish to pursue higher education.
For available apprenticeship offers in the Canton of Vaud and throughout Switzerland, consult the [job offers](nav:jobs) section.

item.title: Vaud Family Allowances: Amounts and How to Apply
item.description: Practical guide to family allowances in the canton of Vaud: how to apply, beneficiaries' rights, required documents and competent compensation fund.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Family allowances: monthly benefit for dependent children, amounts vary by canton - Canton Vaud: specific rights and amounts defined at the cantonal level, can be requested from compensation funds - Procedure: application to be submitted with supporting documents to the competent fund for the economic sector
## Key facts - **What**: Family allowances (Swiss social benefit for families with dependent children) - Where: Each Swiss canton (including Vaud) organizes the system autonomously - Who: Compensation funds for family allowances (cantonal/parity bodies) - Beneficiaries: Parents/guardians of dependent children up to the legal age defined by the canton - Amounts: Vary by canton Vaud and number of children (consult the competent Vaud office for current 2026 data)
Family allowances are a fundamental institution of Swiss social security structured at the cantonal level. Each canton, including Vaud, manages the disbursement of these monthly benefits aimed at parents and guardians of dependent children autonomously. In Vaud, as in all Swiss cantons, family allowances represent an important supplement to family income for those with dependent charges and are an integral part of the social protection system dedicated to families.
The family allowances system in Switzerland operates through specialized compensation funds, public or parity bodies that collect contributions from employers and pay benefits to eligible beneficiaries. Unlike other social benefits managed at the federal level (such as old-age and survivors' insurance AVS/AHV), family allowances remain primarily a cantonal competence. This means that amounts, eligibility conditions, procedures, and age brackets vary from canton to canton, with Vaud having defined its own specific rules and amounts.
### Who is entitled to family allowances
In Vaud, as in the rest of Switzerland, parents or guardians of dependent children who meet specific income, employment, and age conditions are entitled to family allowances. The main categories of beneficiaries include private sector employees, cantonal and municipal public employees, and in certain cases, self-employed workers and farmers.
The maximum age of children for whom allowances are received varies by Swiss canton: generally, allowances are paid until the end of vocational training (apprenticeship) or higher education, or until a certain age threshold (commonly 25 years). In Vaud, a basic monthly amount per child is recognized, with possible supplements for special situations (single-parent family, children in apprenticeship, etc.).
Family allowances do not constitute part of the gross salary and are not subject to deductions for taxes or mandatory insurance. It is a universal social benefit, paid regardless of the amount of salary received (although sometimes subject to income checks for self-employed workers in some cantons). The exact amounts for 2026 in Vaud are not specified in the present source: for current data, it is essential to contact the competent compensation fund for the applicant's work sector or the competent Vaud cantonal office for family welfare. In the canton of Vaud, as in the rest of Switzerland, family allowances are managed by compensation funds (caisse de compensation pour allocations familiales in French). These are specialized entities, generally with a public or paritarian structure (with representations of employers and employees), operating at the cantonal, supra-communal, or sectoral level. Their function is to collect contributions from employers (for each employee) and pay monthly allowances to eligible beneficiaries.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to apply: the first step
The procedure to request family allowances in Vaud begins with identifying the compensation fund competent for your economic sector. The first step is to contact your employer or the relevant trade union: they can provide the name, address, and contacts of the fund designated for your sector. Alternatively, direct recourse to the Vaud cantonal office responsible for social security (Office cantonal de la famille, or equivalent structure of the competent department) allows you to receive complete information and be directed to the correct fund.
### Required documentation
For the submission of the application, the standard documentation usually includes: birth declaration of the children or updated civil status certificate; valid identity document of the applicant; proof of parenthood and cohabitation (e.g., school medical expense receipts, school enrollments, official letters with home addresses); income and employment proofs (recent pay slips, employment letters) — sometimes required by the employer; copy of the Vaud cantonal tax decision of the previous year (in the case of self-employed workers).
### Timeline and deadlines
The application can be submitted at any time of the year, but the allowances are generally backdated to the first day of the month in which the child was born or the applicant started working in the Vaud canton. The processing time normally varies from 2 to 8 weeks from the receipt of the complete application with documentation.
During processing, the fund contacts the employer (if the applicant is an employee) to confirm enrollment, working conditions, and the start date of employment. Family allowances do not require annual renewal but are paid continuously until the condition of right ceases (child reaches the age limit, changes economic sector, moves out of the canton, etc.). However, the fund may request periodic documentary updates (every 2-3 years) to verify the conditions of permanence.
Promptly communicating changes in situation (new child, job change, move, income modification) is essential to avoid recoveries of sums wrongly received. To integrate your calculation of net family income considering family allowances, [consult our salary calculator](nav:calculator). For comparative assessments on the cost of living and other family-related subsidies in Switzerland, visit the [cost of living tool](nav:cost-of-living).

item.title: Apprenticeship and vocational training in the canton of Glarus
item.description: How to find an internship, enter into a contract, learn about the apprentice's salary and achieve professional maturity in the canton of Glarus.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - An EFA apprenticeship lasts 3-4 years depending on the field, alternating between school-based and practical training in a company. - The apprenticeship contract is mandatory by law and regulated by the Code of Obligations. - The salary depends on the canton, the professional field, and the year of apprenticeship; there is no uniform federal minimum wage. - The professional maturity is a complementary certificate that allows access to higher technical schools.
## Key facts - **What**: Dual professional training path with a written contract, lessons in vocational school, and practical training in a company - Where: Canton of Glarus, like all Swiss cantons, offers programs regulated at the federal level - Duration: 3-4 years for EFA, 2 years for practice certificate - Reference law: Federal Law on Vocational and Professional Education and Training and Code of Obligations articles 344-346 - Institutions: Cantonal Office for Vocational Education and Training, professional associations, SEFRI
Apprenticeship in Switzerland is a proven model that combines theoretical education with direct practical training in a company. In the Canton of Glarus, as in the rest of Switzerland, the path is based on the Federal Law on Vocational and Professional Education and Training and allows young people to acquire nationally recognized professional skills. There are two main options: the EFA (Federal Certificate of Competence), which lasts 3-4 years depending on the chosen field, and the practice certificate, a 2-year path mainly oriented towards company practice.
In both cases, the apprenticeship contract must be concluded in writing between the apprentice (or the person exercising parental responsibility if a minor), the company, and, in some cases, a vocational school or training center. The apprentice's salary varies significantly depending on the reference canton, the professional field, and the year of apprenticeship. There is no uniform federal minimum wage for apprentices in Switzerland, so each canton and field applies its own regulations. In the Canton of Glarus, the amounts are determined by collective agreements and specific cantonal directives.
### How to find an apprenticeship in the Canton of Glarus The search for an apprenticeship position begins with the identification of the professional field of interest. Offers can be found through various channels: cantonal databases, specialized job listing websites, portals of professional associations, and direct contacts with local companies. The Cantonal Office for Vocational Education and Training of the Canton of Glarus provides free advice and information on companies offering apprenticeships in various sectors.
Once the company has been identified, the candidate must formally apply with a curriculum vitae, cover letter, and school certificates. If the application is successful, a written apprenticeship contract is concluded before the start of the activity. ### The apprenticeship contract and the apprentice's rights
The apprenticeship contract is governed by Articles 344-346 of the Federal Code of Obligations and must contain essential information: names and addresses of the parties, start date and duration, professional branch, working hours, remuneration, amounts for tools and work clothes, and other specific conditions.
Once signed, the contract imposes mutual rights and obligations. The apprentice has the right to receive adequate training, timely remuneration, a safe working environment in accordance with federal workplace safety regulations, and access to vocational school for mandatory lessons. They also have the right to a minimum of 5 weeks of vacation per year if under 20 years old, and 4 weeks for others. The maximum working hours are set at 9 hours per day and 45 hours per week — limits lower than those for adults, reflecting the need to protect young apprentices.
The company, on the other hand, has the right to expect dedication, commitment, and adherence to company rules. Both parties can terminate the contract during the first year without notice; after that, termination follows specific regulations defined by the Federal Vocational and Professional Education and Training Act.
### The apprentice's remuneration: cantonal and branch variability
Remuneration is one of the most requested pieces of information by candidates and their families. Without a uniform federal minimum wage, remuneration is determined by collective agreements between employers' associations and trade unions, and by specific cantonal directives.
In the canton of Glarus, remuneration depends on three factors: the professional branch (some sectors such as finance, healthcare, and construction pay more than retail or gastronomy); the year of apprenticeship (the salary increases progressively from the first to subsequent years); and the collective agreements applicable in the sector (many sectors have signed agreements that set minimum wages for apprentices of each year). To know the amounts in the canton of Glarus and in the branch of interest, it is advisable to contact the Cantonal Office for Vocational Education and Training, the relevant industry associations, or consult the applicable collective agreements. Training must be in accordance with the Federal Act on Occupational Safety and must protect the apprentice from dangerous or excessively burdensome tasks. Safety regulations are monitored by the competent cantonal authority.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Professional Maturity: The Step Towards Higher Levels
After obtaining the Federal Vocational Education and Training (VET) Certificate, many apprentices choose to continue with the professional maturity, a complementary certificate that recognizes a higher level of general and technical education. Professional maturity allows access to universities of applied sciences (UAS) and some university programs. It can be pursued simultaneously with the apprenticeship (integrated variant) or subsequently (separate variant). In the canton of Glarus, the modalities and providers of professional maturity are indicated by the cantonal office for vocational education and training.
### Step-by-Step Procedure to Apply for an Internship
**Step 1** — Identify the sector: choose the professional sector of interest (mechanics, pharmacy, commerce, IT, electronics, etc.). Step 2 — Research companies: consult job portals and professional association websites to find companies offering internships in your sector. Step 3 — Prepare the application: write a resume, cover letter, and gather school certificates. Step 4 — Apply: send your application to the chosen companies and participate in interviews. Step 5 — Sign the contract: once accepted, sign the written internship contract with the company. Step 6 — Start the apprenticeship: attend vocational school and perform practical activities in the company according to the official training plan.
### Cantonal Support and Resources
The cantonal office for vocational education and training of the canton of Glarus provides free counseling to parents and interested young people. It offers information on available positions, collective agreements, indicative salaries, and funding or contributions for apprentices in financial difficulty. At the federal level, the State Secretariat for Education, Research and Innovation (SERI) provides information on legal rights and duties, as well as access to national internship search platforms.
To assess your economic position and understand how the apprentice salary might impact your personal budget, it is useful to use [salary calculators](nav:calculator) that allow you to simulate net incomes according to cantonal and federal taxes. This tool allows you to plan the internship period and expected income with greater awareness.

item.title: Apprenticeship and training: how it works in Switzerland
item.description: Find out how apprenticeships work in Switzerland: from traineeship research to contract, from pay to legal protections to professional maturity.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Dual apprenticeship: 3-4 years of company practice + vocational school - Federal legal protection: maximum hours, minimum holidays, mandatory social contributions - Nationally recognized Practical Training Certificate (CFC) - Subsequent access to professional maturity and university education
## Key facts - **What**: Dual professional training (practice + theoretical teaching) with CFC certificate - Duration: 3-4 years depending on the sector and type of certificate - Where: Every canton (including Glarus), at registered companies and recognized vocational schools - Who: Apprentices, companies, vocational schools, Cantonal Training Offices - Protection: Wage rights, maximum hours, minimum holidays, mandatory social insurances (AVS/AI/LAINF)
Apprenticeship represents the main professional training path in Switzerland, a dual system that combines practical training in a company with theoretical teaching in a school. In every canton, including Glarus, thousands of companies offer apprenticeship positions in various sectors: from commerce to craftsmanship, from industry to services and healthcare.
Those who undertake an apprenticeship work in a company registered in the cantonal lists, learning a trade under the guidance of a training master. At the same time, they attend general and theoretical training lessons at a recognized vocational school, usually 1-2 days a week. The total duration is usually 3 or 4 years, depending on the sector and the type of certificate pursued.
### Structure and certification
The path allows obtaining a Practical Training Certificate (CFC), recognized at the national level and spendable on the Swiss job market. After the CFC, those who wish can access professional maturity, a title that opens the doors to professional universities (SUP) without an admission exam. There is also the Basic Certificate (CFP), a 2-year path aimed at those with learning difficulties.
Apprenticeship is regulated by federal legislation on professional training, which sets common standards for the whole of Switzerland. However, each canton has competence on local organizational details and supervision of training, through the respective Cantonal Office of Professional Training.
### Legal protection of the worker
As an employee, the apprentice is protected by federal labor law norms. They cannot be exploited: the weekly working hours are limited (maximum 45 hours in industry, offices, and sales; 50 hours in other sectors), the minimum holidays are guaranteed (4 weeks per year, 5 if a minor), and the weekly rest is inviolable. During their stay at the company, the apprentice receives a salary agreed upon in the apprenticeship contract, from which social security contributions are deducted.
Social security contributions (AVS/AI/IPG, LAINF/LAA) are mandatory and paid by the employer or deducted from the salary according to contractual modalities. Health insurance (LAMal/KVG), which in Switzerland is private and mandatory for residents, remains the responsibility of the apprentice (with possible cantonal subsidies for young people with low income).
At the conclusion of the apprenticeship, the CFC is issued, a fundamental document for any subsequent employment in the sector. ### Compensation and salary bands
During the apprenticeship, compensation varies significantly depending on the sector, the cantonal region, and the year of training. There is no federal minimum wage in Switzerland, but many cantons have introduced their own. Additionally, some sectors have collective labor agreements that set minimum wages for apprentices, often with predetermined annual increases.
Generally, the initial salary is lower than that of a qualified worker with the same CFC, but it increases progressively over the years of training. Part of the workday is dedicated to school attendance, during which the apprentice is not physically at the company but still receives compensation. Sometimes the pay slip separately lists practical work days and school days.
### Social contributions and mandatory insurance
The employer automatically pays social security contributions. The apprentice's share for AVS/AI/IPG is 5.3%, while the total (including the employer's contribution) is 10.6%. The work accident insurance (LAINF/LAA) varies by sector (from about 0.7% to 1.5%) and is entirely the company's responsibility.
Health insurance is private: the apprentice must take out insurance within 3 months of the first day of work, choosing a fund from the many available in the canton of residence. There are different deductibles (from CHF 300 to CHF 2500 annually) and coverage models. Each canton offers forms of subsidy for young people with low income. To verify the calculation of your gross-net salary based on social contributions, consult the [salary calculator](nav:calculator).
### Apprenticeship contract: rights and obligations
The apprenticeship contract is a mandatory legal document that must contain: - Start date and total duration of the apprenticeship - Monthly (or daily) salary - Weekly work schedule and school attendance days - Number of annual vacation days (minimum 4 weeks, 5 if a minor) - Duration of the probationary period (usually 1-2 months) - Cause and manner of early termination - Identification of the apprenticeship master and the vocational school
Once the probationary period is over, the contract cannot be terminated by either party without just cause (disciplinary reasons, insolvency, significant change in circumstances). If there is a disagreement about termination, the cantonal conciliation office can intervene.
### Minors and additional protections
If the apprentice is a minor, Swiss law provides additional protections: reduced hours compared to adults, absolute prohibition of night work and particularly dangerous tasks, and mandatory supervision by the apprenticeship master. The minimum vacation increases to 5 weeks per year for those under 20 at the time of signing the contract.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to find an internship
The first step is to identify the sector and the profession of interest. In Switzerland, thousands of professions are accessible through apprenticeships, from bricklayers to nurses, from cooks to electricians, from logistics to graphic designers. Each canton has an official catalog of learnable trades.
The main search channels are: - **National online portals**: many cantons manage websites where all available internship ads are published, organized by sector and location. - Cantonal training office: contact the canton's office directly where you wish to follow the internship (e.g., the one in Glarus for local internships). It provides guidance and lists accredited companies. - Local companies: go directly to companies in the sector of interest with a CV and cover letter, even if they do not have published ads. - School guidance: secondary schools offer professional guidance services and report local opportunities. - Trade associations: professional orders, unions, and sectoral associations often publish ads and maintain lists of training companies.
Once you have found an interesting ad, prepare a professional application: a concise cover letter explaining the chosen motivation, an updated CV, and possibly a professional photograph. The candidate highlights transferable skills (seriousness, punctuality, ability to learn, teamwork) rather than technical qualifications (which will be acquired during the internship).
### Selection and signing of the contract
Companies select apprentices through interviews, sometimes preceded by an aptitude test or skills (reasoning, manual skills, etc.). During the interview, motivation towards the profession, interest in the company and sector, and teamwork attitude are evaluated.
If accepted by the selection, the candidate and the company sign the internship contract in triplicate (one for the young person, one for the company, one for the cantonal office). Before the first working day, the apprentice must: take out the mandatory health insurance (at the company's request), enroll in the canton's vocational school, and find out about the days and times of lessons.
### Professional Maturity: continuing studies
After obtaining the CFC, those who wish to continue towards tertiary education can access the professional maturity. This title requires 1-2 additional years of training, followed in parallel or subsequently to the CFC, and allows direct enrollment in professional universities (SUP) without an admission exam.
Professional maturity is offered by most cantonal vocational training schools and covers various orientations: technical, commercial, social services, health, design, tourism. Access depends on school results during the apprenticeship.
To find internship ads in your area, consult the national internship search portal and contact the cantonal vocational training office directly. If you have already started an apprenticeship, you can check your gross-net salary with the [salary calculator](nav:calculator).

item.title: Volkswagen cuts another 50,000 jobs
item.description: The Volkswagen Group has announced a restructuring plan that envisages the cutting of an additional 50,000 jobs by 2030.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Volkswagen to cut 50,000 jobs by 2030 - Total job losses: 100,000 (15% of global workforce) - Restructuring plan approved by management and unions
## Key facts - **What**: Volkswagen to cut 50,000 jobs - When: By 2030 - Where: Production sites in Emden, Zwickau, Hannover (VW) and Neckarsulm (Audi) - Who: Volkswagen Group - Amount: 100,000 jobs in total
Volkswagen has announced a harsh restructuring plan that involves cutting an additional 50,000 jobs by 2030. This brings the total job losses to 100,000, approximately 15% of the global workforce. The plan was approved on Thursday and agreed upon by management and unions.
The most affected production sites will be those in Emden, Zwickau, Hannover for VW, and Neckarsulm for Audi. There is no talk of closing these plants at the moment, but the possibility remains on the table.
### Implications for the Volkswagen Group
In addition to reducing the workforce, the “Future Plan 2030” aims to halve its model range by 2035. According to the economic magazine Wirtschaftswoche, Volkswagen could withdraw the Spanish brand Seat from the market, with its closure expected by 2029 at the latest.
Chairman of the Supervisory Board Hans Dieter Pötsch stated that the implementation of the new plan “will ensure the long-term sustainability and competitiveness of the Volkswagen Group.” ## Practical Analysis
Volkswagen's restructuring plan has significant implications not only for the group's employees but also for the global automotive industry. The reduction in the range of models and the possible closure of the Seat brand could have repercussions on the electric and hybrid vehicle market, sectors in which Volkswagen is heavily investing.
### Impact on Production Sites
The production sites in Emden, Zwickau, Hannover, and Neckarsulm will be the most affected. Although immediate closures are not being discussed, the possibility remains on the table, which could lead to further uncertainty for workers and local communities.
### Future of Brands
The possible closure of the Seat brand by 2029 could have a significant impact on the market for compact and affordable vehicles. Seat is known for its economical and innovative models, and its disappearance could leave a void in this market segment.
### Sustainability and Competitiveness
Chairman of the Supervisory Board Hans Dieter Pötsch emphasized that the new plan will ensure the long-term sustainability and competitiveness of the Volkswagen Group. This implies that the group is seeking to better position itself in the global market, despite current difficulties.
### Comparison with the Previous Situation
Before the announcement of the restructuring plan, Volkswagen had already cut 50,000 jobs. The current plan brings the total to 100,000, representing a significant reduction in the global workforce. This comparison shows the extent of the measures taken by the group to address current economic challenges.
